courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
question: You fine-tune a 7B model with Adam but freeze all but 1% of its weights. Which part of the 107.8 GB shrinks the most?
options: The 16-bit copy of the frozen weights, because frozen weights are not loaded
Nothing changes, because Adam allocates state for every weight in the model
Gradients and Adam states, because they are only needed for trainable weights
Activations, because a frozen layer does not store activations
explain: Frozen weights still have to sit in memory for the forward pass, and activations are still needed to backpropagate into trainable parts. But gradients and the three fp32 optimizer tensors exist only for trainable parameters, so 14 of the 16 bytes per parameter disappear for the frozen 99%.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: A team wants to teach Llama-2-7B a new programming language by training on 20B tokens of raw source code, and to keep its English skills. What does the evidence suggest?
options: LoRA at r = 16 will match full fine-tuning and forget nothing
Full fine-tuning will likely learn the domain better, while LoRA preserves more of the base skills; pick based on which matters more
Prompt tuning is the best choice because it has the fewest parameters
Rank does not matter in continued pretraining
explain: In Biderman et al.'s continued pretraining runs, full fine-tuning outperformed every LoRA rank on the target domain, and LoRA forgot less. That is a real tradeoff, not a free lunch, and rank clearly ordered LoRA's results.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
question: Your unlearned model gets a TOFU forget quality (KS-test p-value) of 0.0004. What does that mean?
options: The model forgot 99.96% of the forget set
The model's utility is 0.0004
The model is statistically indistinguishable from the retain model
The truth-ratio distribution on the forget set is very unlikely to come from the same distribution as the retain model's, so unlearning is incomplete or overshot
explain: Forget quality is the p-value of a two-sample KS test between the unlearned and retain models' truth-ratio distributions. A tiny p-value means the distributions clearly differ, which is poor unlearning in either direction. It is not a percentage of facts forgotten.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
question: Why use a simulated internet (INetSim, FakeNet-NG) instead of no network at all?
options: It makes the malware run faster
It is required by law
The sample often reveals its domains and protocols only when something answers, and nothing real is reached
It hides the analysis VM from the malware
explain: With no network, many samples stall at their first lookup. A fake service answers, so you capture the domains, URLs and protocol the sample uses, while nothing leaves the lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Disassemblers and decompilers: from bytes back to C
question: A decompiler shows `if (local_14 < 0x5a)` but you suspect a signed versus unsigned mistake matters for a size check. What should you do?
options: Trust the decompiler; it is always exact
Rename local_14 and move on
Check the conditional jump in the disassembly: jl or jg mean signed, jb or ja mean unsigned
Rerun the decompiler with a different font
explain: The jump instruction is the ground truth for signedness. Decompilers guess types; when the detail matters, confirm in assembly.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
question: Why did notes.txt not match, even though it contains both the banner and the URL?
options: YARA cannot read .txt files
The condition requires uint16(0) == 0x5A4D, and the text file does not start with MZ
The filesize was too large
nocase only works on PE files
explain: The condition combines file structure and content. A text file that quotes the strings fails the structural check, which is exactly the false positive the check was added to prevent.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
question: With a Matryoshka model you shortlist with 2-d prefixes and keep the top 3 documents. In the toy, which statement is true?
options: The shortlist is B, A, C, so the true best match A survives, and the 8-d rerank puts A first
The shortlist is A, B, C in exact final order, so no rerank is needed
The shortlist is C, B, A, so A is lost
A 2-d prefix cannot be used for search at all
explain: At m = 2 the Matryoshka scores are B 1.000, A 1.000, C 0.998: the right documents, in blurred order. Reranking those three at m = 8 gives A 0.997, B 0.757, C 0.616. A shortlist needs to contain the right items, not order them perfectly.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
question: Why did Megatron adopt 1F1B (PipeDream-Flush) over GPipe even though both have the same bubble?
options: 1F1B needs no pipeline flush
1F1B sends fewer bytes between stages
1F1B caps in-flight microbatches at p instead of m, so activation memory stops growing with the number of microbatches
1F1B lets each microbatch use slightly stale weights, which is faster
explain: The bubble is (p-1)/m for both. GPipe stores activations for all m microbatches; 1F1B starts backward passes early and never has more than p outstanding. This is what makes a large m (small bubble) affordable.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
question: A team patches their allocator from 4 to 8 classes per doubling. Which outcome should they expect?
options: Total memory always falls by about 9%
External fragmentation disappears because rounding is smaller
Allocation becomes slower because each request must search all classes
Worst-case internal waste falls from about 20% to about 11%, with more partly empty slabs to offset part of the gain
explain: Worst-case waste is just under 1/(n+1): 20% for n = 4, 11% for n = 8. But twice as many classes means twice as many places for partly filled slabs and cached objects to sit, so the net saving depends on the workload. Class lookup stays a computation, not a search.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
question: Ten threads each run `counter.fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` 1000 times; then main joins all ten and reads the counter. What does main see?
options: Exactly 10000
Any value from 1000 to 10000, since Relaxed does not order the increments
10000 on x86 but possibly less on ARM64
Undefined behavior, because Relaxed operations race
explain: Each fetch_add is atomic, so none are lost, and all of them sit in one modification order. Joining a thread creates happens-before from everything it did to the code after the join, so main reads the final value. Relaxed is not a race: races need a non-atomic access.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: A shutdown flag is set by one thread and polled by workers, which simply exit their loop when they see it. No other data is passed through the flag. Which ordering fits?
options: SeqCst, to make sure workers see it quickly
Release store and Acquire load
Relaxed
AcqRel on both store and load
explain: The flag carries no other data, so no happens-before edge is needed: Relaxed gives atomicity, and the model says nothing about speed anyway. If the workers had to read results or config written before the flag, you would upgrade to Release and Acquire. AcqRel is only for read-modify-write operations.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
question: CPU 1 calls synchronize_rcu() at time 10. Reader X started at time 8 and ends at 12; reader Y starts at 11 and ends at 30. Ignoring batching delays, when may synchronize_rcu() return?
options: At 30, after both readers
At 12, after X; Y need not be waited for
At 10, immediately, because readers take no locks
At 11, when Y starts
explain: Only pre-existing read-side critical sections count. X was running at time 10, so the grace period must cover it. Y started after the removal and cannot have obtained the removed pointer, so waiting for it would be wasted. Real implementations may return somewhat later because they batch requests.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Stack buffer overflow: when a copy runs past the end
question: Which change fixes `strcpy(buf, name)` for `char buf[8]` without silently corrupting memory for long names?
options: Make buf 64 bytes so normal names fit
Call strcpy twice to check the result
Use strncpy(buf, name, sizeof buf) and nothing else
Use snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%s", name), or reject names with strlen(name) >= sizeof buf
explain: A bigger buffer only raises the bar: a 65-byte name still overflows. strncpy stops at the size but leaves buf unterminated for long names, so the next read runs off the end. snprintf truncates and terminates; an explicit length check rejects the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
question: Code does `uint32_t n = w * h * 4; char *px = malloc(n);` for an image of width w and height h from a file, then writes w*h*4 bytes. What is the bug?
options: None: malloc checks the size
The bug is only that malloc's result is not checked
malloc can't allocate images
w * h * 4 can wrap in 32 bits, so px is smaller than the bytes later written
explain: For a large enough w and h the product exceeds 4,294,967,295 and wraps, so the allocation is small. The later writes use the true size and overflow. Checking malloc's result for NULL does not help because malloc succeeds. Fix: check each multiplication (calloc or __builtin_mul_overflow) and limit w and h.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Finding memory bugs: warnings, sanitizers, Valgrind and fuzzing
question: Why is AddressSanitizer usually not enabled in production builds?
options: It only works on Windows
Its documentation says the runtime is a testing tool not designed for security-sensitive production use, and it costs about 2x speed and more memory
It produces many false alarms
It removes bounds checks
explain: ASan is precise (its docs say no false alarms) but slows programs about 2x, uses extra memory, and its runtime was not built with production security constraints in mind. It belongs in testing, CI and fuzzing.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
question: You switch from batch hard to batch all without changing anything else and validation mAP drops. Which change would most directly test the 'washed out' explanation?
options: Increase the margin to 1.0
Average the loss only over triplets with non-zero loss
Square the distances
Use K = 1
explain: If zero-loss triplets dilute the gradient, averaging only the active terms removes the dilution. Hermans and colleagues ran this test and the non-zero average performed much better than the plain average.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
question: A new hash map is 2x faster than the old one in a benchmark with 1000 keys, but the service using 50 million keys sees no gain. What is the most plausible reason?
options: At 1000 keys both maps fit in cache, so the benchmark measured hashing and probing on hot data; at 50 million keys both are dominated by cache misses to DRAM
The benchmark forgot DoNotOptimize
The service has more threads
Hash maps are O(1), so size cannot matter
explain: A small key set keeps the whole table in L1 or L2, where instruction counts dominate. A huge table makes nearly every probe a DRAM miss, and a design that saves instructions but makes as many misses gains little. Big-O hides exactly this constant. Sweep the size before trusting the 2x.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
question: An agentic batch has 8 trajectories per group; one takes 40 turns while the rest finish in 3. Which setting keeps engine slots busiest while that trajectory runs?
options: --rollout-submission-granularity group, so the group stays together
--pause-generation-mode abort, to kill stragglers
--update-weights-interval 0
--rollout-submission-granularity sample, so each finished trajectory frees its own slot
explain: With sample granularity, the seven short trajectories free their slots as soon as they finish, and new groups start in them. With group granularity, all eight slots stay reserved until the 40-turn trajectory returns. Abort mode is rejected under fully async.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
question: A 3-slot cache holds X, Y and Z. Their next requests are: X in 7 requests, Y never, Z in 2 requests. A miss for W arrives. What does Belady's MIN evict?
options: Z, because it was used least recently
X, because it is needed later than Z
Y, because it is never requested again
W is not admitted, because MIN only evicts on hits
explain: MIN evicts the object whose next request is furthest away, and never counts as furthest of all. Recency (option one) is LRU's rule, not MIN's. X is a reasonable second choice but loses to Y.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
question: Using Lykouris and Vassilvitskii's result, what happens to their predictor-augmented Marker algorithm if the oracle's predictions become arbitrarily bad?
options: It stays within O(log k) of optimal, the same bound as classic Marker without predictions
Its competitive ratio grows without bound
It becomes exactly as good as Belady's MIN
It refuses to evict
explain: The point of the construction is robustness: the ratio improves as prediction error falls, but it is always capped by O(log k), which is achievable with no oracle at all. Blindly following the oracle has no such cap.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Decoupled RoPE: why position breaks absorption
question: Why is the decoupled RoPE key $k^R_t$ shared across all heads, while the RoPE query $q^R_{t,i}$ is per head?
options: Keys must be cached and queries do not; sharing the key keeps the cache at $d_c + d_h^R$ instead of $d_c + n_h d_h^R$
Because RoPE only works with a single head
To save FLOPs on the query side
Because the latent already contains position
explain: Queries are computed for the current token only and discarded, so per-head queries cost no cache. A per-head key would add $n_h d_h^R = 8192$ elements per token per layer in DeepSeek-V3.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
question: A batch of 64 decode rows is spread across 64 different adapters. According to Punica's roofline analysis, what limits the SGMV kernel?
options: Tensor Core throughput, because there are 64 matmuls
Memory bandwidth, because each row reads its own adapter weights and does little math per byte
PCIe bandwidth (the CPU-to-GPU bus), because adapters are always loaded from the CPU
Nothing: the cost is identical to one shared adapter
explain: With n = s_n the I/O term n h_i h_o grows with the batch, so arithmetic intensity stays about 0.94 FLOPs per byte, firmly bandwidth bound. Measured latency rose from 37 to 116 microseconds, versus 37 to 40 for a single shared adapter.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: You configure LlamaIndex `QueryFusionRetriever(num_queries=4, ...)` with one retriever. How many LLM-generated queries and how many searches does one call make?
options: 4 generated, 4 searches
4 generated, 5 searches
3 generated, 4 searches
1 generated, 4 searches
explain: num_queries counts the original. The prompt asks the LLM for num_queries - 1 = 3 queries, and the original plus those 3 are each searched once per retriever: 4 searches. Setting num_queries=1 disables generation.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
question: The LLM sometimes returns phrasings that shift the question to a neighboring topic. Which change most directly limits the damage?
options: Raise N so the drifted phrasing is outvoted
Keep the original query in the set and inspect or filter generated queries that look off-topic
Replace RRF with an unranked union
Drop the original query to avoid bias
explain: The original query cannot drift and anchors fusion. Filtering clearly off-topic rewrites (or constraining the prompt) removes the junk list. Raising N adds cost and may add more drift; a union passes drifted results straight through.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: RankGPT reranks M = 100 passages with w = 20 and s = 10. You switch to w = 20, s = 5 to give passages more chances to move. How many LLM calls does one pass now make?
explain: ceil((100 - 20) / 5) + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17 calls, reading 17 x 20 = 340 passages. Smaller steps mean more overlap and almost double the cost of s = 10. The guaranteed-correct top also grows, from w - s = 10 to 15.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: At depth k = 2 in DeepSeek-V3's scheme, which inputs does the module use for position i, and which token does it predict?
options: h_i from the main model and Emb(t_i+1); predicts t_i+2
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+3); predicts t_i+3
Only Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
explain: Depth k combines h at depth k - 1 with the embedding of t(i+k) and predicts t(i+k+1). For k = 2 that is h from depth 1, Emb(t(i+2)), and target t(i+3).

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
question: A colleague raises Muon's Newton-Schulz steps from 5 to 10 to get a more exactly orthogonal update. Based on the Moonlight report, what should they expect?
options: Noticeably lower loss, since the update is now exactly U V-transpose
Divergence, because the tuned polynomial is unstable after 5 steps
A more accurate orthogonalization but no better model, at twice the Newton-Schulz cost
No change at all in the update, because the iteration converged after 5 steps
explain: Moonlight reports that $N = 10$ gives a more accurate orthogonalization than $N = 5$ but does not improve performance, so they kept 5. With the tuned coefficients the values keep bouncing within roughly $[0.7, 1.2]$, so the update does change, just not in a way that helps.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
question: You train a hidden d x d layer with Adam. You widen d from 1024 to 4096 and want the per-coordinate change of $\Delta W\,x$ after one step to stay the same. What should the layer's learning rate do?
options: Stay the same, because Adam already normalizes gradients
Be divided by 4, the width ratio
Be divided by 2, the square root of the width ratio
Be multiplied by 4
explain: Adam makes each entry of $\Delta W$ about $\pm\eta$ regardless of width, and $\Delta W$ is aligned with $x$, so $\Delta W\,x$ entries scale like $\eta \cdot \text{fan\_in}$. Keeping them fixed when fan_in grows 4x means dividing $\eta$ by 4. The square-root rule would be right for random, uncorrelated matrices, not for updates.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
question: A colleague writes unlock as `locked.store(false, Relaxed)` to save a few cycles. Lock still uses `swap(true, Acquire)`. What can go wrong?
options: The next owner may not see writes made inside the previous critical section
Two threads can own the lock at once
Nothing: Acquire on the lock side is enough
The lock can never be acquired again
explain: Mutual exclusion still holds, because the swap is atomic regardless of ordering. What breaks is visibility: without a Release store there is no happens-before edge from the old owner's writes to the new owner's reads, so the new owner may read stale data.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
question: Kernel code running in an interrupt handler needs to protect a counter shared with a normal kernel thread. Which lock fits?
options: struct mutex, because it spins optimistically first
A futex
A spin lock taken with interrupts disabled (for example spin_lock_irqsave) on the thread side
No lock: interrupts cannot run concurrently with threads
explain: Interrupt handlers cannot sleep, so sleeping locks like mutex are out. The thread side must also disable interrupts while holding the spin lock, or the interrupt could fire on the same CPU and spin forever on a lock its own CPU holds.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
question: Two Serializable transactions each run SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id = <own id> on a table with no index on id, then UPDATE their own, different row. PostgreSQL aborts one even though no serial order would differ. Why?
options: SSI blocked on an SIRead lock and the lock timed out
A deadlock between the two updates
Read Committed was used by mistake
A false positive: each sequential scan took a relation-level SIRead lock, so each update formed an rw edge with the other's read
explain: SIRead locks never block, so there is no timeout or deadlock. Without an index the SELECT uses a sequential scan, which locks the whole relation, so the other transaction's update of a different row still looks like an rw conflict. Edges both ways form a dangerous structure even though neither read cared about the other row. An index on id would avoid it.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
question: A tagger predicts `B-PER I-PER` over the three tokens `Mary Jane Smith` where gold is one PER spanning all three. What does this contribute to the entity-level counts?
options: 1 TP, since two of three tokens are inside the right entity
1 TP and 1 FP, for getting the type right but the end wrong
0.67 TP under partial credit
1 FP and 1 FN, because the predicted span is not in the gold set and the gold span was not predicted
explain: Exact match has no partial credit. PER(0,1) is not PER(0,2), so the prediction is a false positive and the gold entity is a false negative. One wrong boundary tag costs two errors, which is why boundary quality drives entity F1 much harder than token accuracy suggests.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
question: A model uses GQA with 8 query heads per KV group. A sparse method lets each head choose 4 of 64 KV blocks independently, and the heads mostly disagree. During decoding, roughly what happens to memory traffic per group?
options: It drops to 4/64 of dense, since each head reads 4 blocks
It drops to somewhere up to 32/64 of dense, because the union of the heads' picks must be loaded
It is unchanged, because sparse methods never reduce memory reads
It increases, because sparse methods must read all keys to score them
explain: Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so the kernel loads the union of their selections: up to 8 x 4 = 32 distinct blocks. Compute per head is 4/64, but decoding is memory bound, so the union is what sets latency. This is exactly why NSA forces one shared selection per group.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
question: During DSA's dense warm-up, what is the indexer trained to predict?
options: The next token, using the language modeling loss
Which tokens NSA's compression branch would select
The main attention distribution for each query, summed over heads and L1-normalized, via a KL loss
A binary label for whether each token is in the top 2048
explain: The target $p_{t,:}$ is the dense main attention summed over heads and normalized. The indexer's softmax is pulled toward it with KL divergence while the main model is frozen, so the indexer learns which tokens the model actually attends to before sparsity is switched on.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
question: In a BK-tree search with radius 2, the current node is at distance 6 from the query. Which children are visited?
options: Children on edges 4 to 8
Only children on edges 0 to 2
All children, because the node did not match
None, because the node did not match
explain: A child on edge e is at distance e from this node, so by the triangle inequality its distance to the query is at least |6 - e|. That is at most 2 only when e is between 4 and 8. Not matching the node itself does not stop the descent.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
question: You want to post-train a model with hundreds of billions of parameters and 16k-token sequences. Which choice matches what the docs recommend?
options: Megatron backend, configured under policy.megatron_cfg, with its optimizer under megatron_cfg.optimizer
Automodel backend with vLLM, since it is the default
Hugging Face generation backend for rollouts
Convert to a Megatron checkpoint by hand and point NeMo RL at it
explain: The training-backends doc positions Megatron for scaling to very large models, and the README lists larger models with longer sequences under Megatron Core parallelisms. NeMo RL takes only HF checkpoints as input and converts them itself, so a hand-made Megatron checkpoint is not the documented path.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
question: DAI is enabled on a VLAN, but a server with a manually configured (static) IP address suddenly cannot be reached. What is the most likely cause?
options: DAI blocks all servers by design
The server's MAC address is too long
DAI only works on trunk ports
The server's ARP packets are dropped because DHCP snooping never saw a lease for it, so it has no binding
explain: DAI validates ARP against the DHCP snooping table. A statically addressed host never leased its address, so its ARP fails the check. The fix is a static binding (or ARP access list) for that host, or a trusted port where appropriate.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Kaminsky 2008: poisoning a whole domain
question: A company patched its resolver to randomise source ports in 2008, but its firewall performs port address translation on outgoing DNS and assigns ports sequentially. What is the effect?
options: None: the resolver's randomness survives translation
The firewall blocks all forged replies
DNS stops working
The firewall makes the outgoing ports predictable again, undoing much of the patch
explain: CERT's note warns that port address translation (PAT) devices rewrite source ports and 'can reduce or eliminate improvements gained by patching DNS software'. The attacker sees the translated port, so predictable translation hands back the 16 bits the patch added.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: SYN floods and SYN cookies
question: A server enables SYN cookies permanently (Linux setting 2) to improve performance under normal heavy load. What does the kernel documentation say about this?
options: It is the recommended setting for busy servers
It has no side effects
It disables the three-way handshake
It is wrong: cookies are a fallback; they lose TCP extensions and can degrade service, so tune the backlog for real load instead
explain: The documentation says syncookies must not be used to help highly loaded servers handle legal connection rates, because they do not allow TCP extensions. Setting 2 exists to test their effect, not as a tuning knob.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
question: A router access list allows 'TCP from any with the ACK flag set' so that replies work. What can an outside attacker do that a stateful firewall would block?
options: Nothing different: both read the ACK flag
Send packets with ACK set to any internal port, which pass because the filter cannot check that a real connection exists; useful for probing and some attacks
Decrypt TLS traffic
Flood the router with SYNs
explain: A stateless filter has no memory of which connections exist, so any packet with ACK set looks like a reply. A stateful firewall checks its table and drops ACKs that belong to no known connection.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
question: A packet's header says it comes from address A. What does that prove about who sent it?
options: It proves the packet came from A, because routers check the sender
It proves the packet came from A's network, but not which device
Nothing by itself: the sender's own software wrote that field
It proves the packet came from A only if the payload is longer than the header
explain: The header is just bytes written by whoever built the packet. Some networks filter packets with impossible source addresses (you will meet this as ingress filtering), but the basic protocols do not verify the sender. Treat a source address as a claim, not a proof.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
question: A router has routes for `208.65.152.0/22` (to A), `208.65.153.0/24` (to B) and `0.0.0.0/0` (to C). Where does it send a packet for `208.65.155.4`?
options: B, because /24 is the longest prefix in the table
C, because only exact matches count
A, because 208.65.155.4 is inside the /22 (152.0 to 155.255) but not inside the /24
It drops the packet as ambiguous
explain: Longest prefix match only chooses among prefixes that actually contain the address. 208.65.152.0/22 spans 208.65.152.0 to 208.65.155.255, so it matches; the /24 covers only 208.65.153.x. The default route also matches but is shorter.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTP: requests, responses, headers and cookies
question: A log shows 3,000 requests in two minutes from one IP, almost all `404 Not Found`, for paths like `/admin`, `/backup.zip`, `/.git/config`. What is most likely happening?
options: A user with a broken bookmark
Automated scanning for forgotten or sensitive files
A denial-of-service attack using amplification
Normal search engine indexing
explain: Thousands of guessed paths in a short time, mostly missing, are the fingerprint of a content discovery scanner looking for admin panels, backups and exposed repositories. The rare 200 among them is the line to investigate first.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A 4-node server's distance table shows 10 on the diagonal and 20 everywhere else. What is the safest reading?
options: Every remote access costs exactly twice a local one
Remote access is roughly twice as costly as local, but firmware tables can be inaccurate, so measure
The machine is actually UMA because all remote entries are equal
explain: SLIT values are relative estimates normalized to 10 for local access. Drepper shows a real table that reported 20 for every pair even though some pairs had to be two hops apart. Use the table as a hint and benchmark when placement matters.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: A database pins each worker to one node and places every buffer with explicit mbind policies. Profiling shows time spent in page faults on pages that never move. What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable MPOL_INTERLEAVE on all buffers
Use smaller pages so faults are cheaper
Disable automatic NUMA balancing for this workload
explain: These are NUMA hinting faults from automatic balancing sampling pages that are already correctly placed. The kernel docs recommend disabling balancing when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
question: A service writes 300 TB per year to a 1 TB drive rated for 10,000 P/E cycles. The drive's FDP statistics show media bytes written are 5x host bytes. Roughly how long until rated wear-out?
options: About 6.7 years
About 33 years
About 1.3 years
Never, wear leveling prevents it
explain: Lifetime host writes = 1 TB x 10,000 / 5 = 2,000 TB. At 300 TB per year that is 2000/300, about 6.7 years. Halving A to 2.5 would double it.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
question: Why does DETR not need NMS at test time?
options: Its object queries are fixed to non-overlapping image regions
It applies NMS inside the transformer decoder
One-to-one Hungarian matching during training gives each object only one positive prediction, so other slots learn to predict 'no object'
It only predicts one object per image
explain: Object queries are learned embeddings, not fixed regions. Because the matching assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one slot, a second slot covering the same object is trained toward the no-object class. The DETR paper reports that adding NMS helps early decoder layers but slightly hurts AP at the last layer.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Batching writes: the cost versus latency dial
question: To cut latency further, an engineer changes the Agent to acknowledge a Produce request as soon as it lands in the in-memory buffer. What does this break?
options: Ordering within a partition
Nothing, since S3 is durable
Compaction, because files get smaller
Durability: if the Agent crashes before the PUT, acknowledged records are lost
explain: The buffer is memory in a stateless process. WarpStream never acknowledges a write until it is in object storage and committed to the metadata store, which is what lets it lose every Agent without losing acknowledged data. Acking from memory turns a crash into data loss.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
question: Checkout p99 reads 1.3 s and the orders database p99 reads 0.9 s, both rising in the same minute. What do the metrics alone establish?
options: That checkout requests are waiting on the database
That the database is the root cause, since it is the deepest component
That the two are correlated in time, but not that any single checkout request waited on the database
Nothing, because percentiles from different services are never comparable
explain: Metrics are per-component aggregates with no request identity, so simultaneity is a hypothesis, not a causal link. The slow checkout requests and the slow queries may even be disjoint sets. A trace carries parent and child spans and settles it for one request.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
question: Why does DBNet replace the hard threshold with a sigmoid of k(P - T)?
options: It makes inference faster than a comparison
It lets gradients flow so the network can learn a per-pixel threshold map
It removes the need for the probability map
It guarantees that adjacent words never merge
explain: A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere, so a threshold inside it cannot be learned. The steep sigmoid approximates the step but stays differentiable. At inference the paper actually drops this path and uses a constant threshold on P.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
question: Which bug is usually the most severe for a multi-user Linux server?
options: A memory bug in a kernel system call that any process can make
A crash in a user's text editor
A memory bug in a setuid program that only root can run
A typo in a log message
explain: A kernel bug reachable from any process can bypass every permission check, for every user and every container on the host. A setuid program that only root can run gives an attacker nothing new.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: AppArmor: path-based profiles that confine one program
question: What is the key design difference between AppArmor and SELinux?
options: AppArmor rules name paths a program uses; SELinux rules name types stored in labels on subjects and objects
AppArmor only works on Windows
SELinux is discretionary and AppArmor is mandatory
AppArmor confines users, SELinux confines programs
explain: Both are mandatory and both confine programs. AppArmor writes rules in terms of paths, which makes profiles readable; SELinux writes them in terms of types, so a file's label travels with it.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Namespaces and cgroups: the building blocks of containers
question: A process is root inside a user namespace (mapped to UID 1000 outside). It tries to set the system's calendar clock. What happens?
options: It succeeds, because it has all capabilities in its namespace
It succeeds only inside a time namespace
It changes the clock only for the container
It fails, because capabilities in a user namespace apply only to resources governed by that namespace, and the system clock is not one
explain: user_namespaces(7) uses this very example: changing the system time is governed by CAP_SYS_TIME in the initial namespace. Time namespaces offset only the boot and monotonic clocks.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs
question: An attacker has root on a server with kernel lockdown enabled and module signature enforcement on. What stops them loading a rootkit module they compiled?
options: Nothing: root can do anything
The rootkit must be in /lib/modules
Secure boot scans the disk at runtime
The kernel refuses modules that are not validly signed with a trusted key, even for root
explain: With enforcement, the kernel itself checks the signature at load time. Root controls the filesystem but does not hold the signing key, so the module is refused.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
question: In the tiny project, you edit ops.h. Which objects recompile?
options: Only add.o and matmul.o, since ops.h declares their functions
add.o, matmul.o and main.o
All 5 objects, because ops.h includes tensor.h
None until you run a clean build
explain: add.cpp, matmul.cpp and main.cpp include ops.h, so 3 of 5 objects recompile. The include edge tensor.h to ops.h points the other way: editing ops.h does not affect files that only include tensor.h, such as tensor.cpp.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
question: A CUDA-heavy project takes 90 minutes to build with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=all. You only need to test on your own CC 8.9 GPU. Which change cuts build time the most while still running locally?
options: Set CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (or 89)
Switch the generator from Ninja to Makefiles
Set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel
Use 89-virtual so the driver compiles at startup
explain: With all, every .cu file is compiled for every supported real architecture plus PTX; a single native target removes nearly all of that repeated device compilation. 89-virtual also builds once, but then every run JIT compiles all kernels at startup, which is slow for a large project.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
question: A maintainer proposes `--reruns 3` globally to fix red CI. Which concern is most serious?
options: Reruns make pytest exit with code 5
A real race condition that fails 50 percent of runs would be reported only $0.5^4 = 6.25$ percent of the time
Reruns are not supported on GitHub Actions
Reruns change the order tests are collected in
explain: With 3 reruns a test is reported failed only if all 4 attempts fail. For a real intermittent bug with $q = 0.5$, that is $0.5^4 = 0.0625$, so about 94 percent of runs would be green despite the bug.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Giving review: reading order and comments that land
question: Which comment is phrased the way this lesson recommends?
options: "You clearly didn't test this."
"Nit: this could be a list comprehension, but the loop is fine too."
"This is wrong."
"Why would anyone write it like this?"
explain: It is labeled (Nit: tells the author it is optional), it is about the code, and it says the existing version is acceptable. The others aim at the person or give no reason and no way forward.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
question: You find a way to read other users' files through a project's upload endpoint. The repo has SECURITY.md and private vulnerability reporting enabled. What do you do?
options: Use the private report (or the channel SECURITY.md names) and follow its instructions
Open a detailed public issue so the fix gets attention quickly
Open a PR with the fix and describe the exploit in the PR body
Post a minimal reproducer in the project's public chat
explain: Public issues, PRs and chat disclose the vulnerability before a fix ships. SECURITY.md gives the project's reporting instructions, and private vulnerability reporting delivers the report only to maintainers.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
question: Halfway through a rebase, Git stops with a conflict in `parser.c` and you are unsure of your fix. Which command returns the branch to exactly where it was before you started?
options: `git rebase --skip`
`git rebase --abort`
`git rebase --continue`
`git reset --hard upstream/main`
explain: `--abort` stops the rebase and restores the original branch. `--skip` drops the conflicting commit and keeps going, which loses that change. `--continue` needs the conflict resolved and staged. Resetting to upstream/main throws away all your commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
question: Your company uses an Apache-2.0 library and later files a patent suit claiming that library infringes one of its patents. What happens under section 3?
options: The patent licenses your company received for that library terminate as of the filing date
The copyright license terminates and you must stop using the code
Nothing, because Apache-2.0 only covers copyright
The library's contributors lose their own patents
explain: Section 3 grants a patent license from each contributor, and it terminates for anyone who starts patent litigation alleging the Work infringes. The copyright license in section 2 is not what terminates.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
question: A project wants contributor provenance with minimal friction for drive-by contributors, and does not need any rights beyond its license. Which fits best?
options: A corporate CLA with each contributor's employer
The DCO with a sign-off check on every commit
An individual CLA signed before any PR is reviewed
No policy, since inbound=outbound needs no record at all
explain: The DCO adds one trailer per commit and no paperwork, while still recording a certification of origin. CLAs suit projects that want an explicit, signed grant (often including patents); no policy leaves no record of who certified the code's origin.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
question: Your search for a function name returns 40 hits, 30 of them under deps/. What is the best next step for a Redis server bug?
options: Read all 40 hits in order
Delete deps/ from your clone so search is faster
Search only the tests
Restrict the search to src, for example `git grep -n name -- src`, since deps is vendored third-party code
explain: Vendored code is a copy of another project. Bugs there are usually fixed upstream, not in this repo. A pathspec after `--` limits git grep to the directories that matter without changing the checkout.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
question: A maintainer replies "works for me" to your report. Which addition is most likely to turn it into a reproduction?
options: A longer description of how important the bug is to your team
The exact versions of the library, Python and OS you ran, plus the input that triggered it as text
A screenshot of the stack trace with the failing line circled
A link to your full private application repository
explain: "Works for me" usually means your environment or input differs from theirs in a way the report did not capture. Exact versions and the triggering input close that gap. A screenshot is not searchable, a private repo is not runnable by them, and urgency does not help them see the bug.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
question: Your repro fails on your GPU machine but passes on the maintainer's CPU-only laptop, even with `torch.manual_seed(0)`. What is the most useful next step?
options: Assume the maintainer made a mistake and ask them to retry
Remove the seed, since it obviously does not help
Report the device and the collect_env output, and check whether the failure needs the GPU path (for example, run your repro on CPU yourself)
explain: PyTorch's notes say results can differ between CPU and GPU even with identical seeds. Checking whether the failure needs the GPU narrows the hidden variable, and the environment report lets the maintainer match your setup.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
question: A request reserves 2048 contiguous slots and finishes after 300 tokens. What kind of waste are the 1748 untouched slots?
options: External fragmentation, because they sit between other requests
Internal fragmentation, because they are inside the request's own chunk and were never used
Reserved slots, because they will be used by later tokens of the same request
No waste, because the allocator frees them when the request ends
explain: They are inside the request's allocation and were never filled, which is internal fragmentation. The paper notes it is only known to be waste after the request finishes. Reserved slots are the ones that will eventually be filled; external fragmentation is space between allocations.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: What a penetration test is, and what it is not
question: A company's board wants to know whether the security team would detect and contain a determined intruder heading for the finance system. Which engagement fits best?
options: A weekly vulnerability scan of all servers
A bug bounty programme
A red team engagement with an objective and an unwarned SOC
A one-day automated web scan
explain: The question is about detection and response, which is what a red team tests: an objective, adversary emulation, and defenders who are not told in advance. Scans and bounties find flaws but do not test the SOC.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: what your DNS tells the world
question: A company's public DNS contains `MX 10 mail.protection.outlook.com.` and a CNAME `status.company.example` pointing to a hosted status page service. What has passive recon told you?
options: The company's email is handled by a Microsoft cloud service and its status page by a third party, both of which need their own permission before any testing
Nothing useful
That the company's mail server is vulnerable
That you may now test Microsoft's mail servers
explain: MX and CNAME records reveal providers. Knowing them shapes scope: those systems belong to third parties, and the client cannot authorise testing them.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: From scan XML to a findings table
question: Why parse Nmap's XML instead of the normal text output?
options: The text output is encrypted
XML is the format the Nmap author recommends for programs: it carries more information, such as method and confidence, and is stable across versions
XML scans are faster
The text output omits open ports
explain: The guide recommends XML for programmatic use because normal output is for humans and changes, while XML is extensible and includes fields such as method and conf.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Kali Linux and what its tool categories are for
question: Which statement about Kali Linux metapackages is accurate?
options: They are encrypted bundles only OffSec can install
Each one is a single large program
They are ordinary packages that pull in a group of tools for one purpose, such as information gathering or reporting
They authorise you to test any system
explain: Kali's documentation describes metapackages as a way to install many packages at once, grouped by purpose. They grant no permission of any kind.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
question: A folded file contains `app;main;run;parse 40` and `app;main;run 10`. What are the self and total sample counts of `run`?
options: self 50, total 50
self 10, total 50
self 0, total 50
self 10, total 10
explain: run is the leaf only in the second line, so self = 10. It appears on the stack in both lines, so total = 40 + 10 = 50.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
question: A server has ADR but not eADR. You map a file on a DAX file system with MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE | MAP_SYNC. Which granularity does libpmem2 report for the mapping?
options: PMEM2_GRANULARITY_CACHE_LINE: flush the touched cache lines, then fence
PMEM2_GRANULARITY_PAGE: you still need msync for durability
PMEM2_GRANULARITY_BYTE: every retired store is already durable
It depends on whether you use CLWB or CLFLUSHOPT
explain: MAP_SYNC succeeded, so the mapping is real persistent memory and PAGE is not needed. Without eADR the caches are outside the protected domain, so the result is CACHE_LINE. BYTE requires the persistence_domain to include cpu_cache. The flush instruction choice does not change the granularity.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Concurrent PM indexes, RECIPE and what Optane measurements showed
question: A lock-free DRAM B+ tree's writers complete any half-finished split they encounter before doing their own work. Which RECIPE condition fits, and what does conversion need?
options: Condition #1: flush and fence after each store only
Condition #3: add a helper mechanism, then flushes and fences
Condition #2: add flushes and fences after stores, and after loads so observed state is persisted first
It cannot be converted, because lock-free indexes never satisfy RECIPE's conditions
explain: Writers that fix inconsistencies they find are Condition #2, like BwTree. The helper already exists, so recovery after a crash is just another writer finishing the job; conversion adds flushes and fences after stores and loads.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: How an email actually moves: SMTP and MX records
question: In the SMTP session, which command sets the address that bounces are sent to?
options: RCPT TO
EHLO
MAIL FROM
The From: header inside DATA
explain: MAIL FROM sets the envelope sender, also called the reverse-path; bounce messages go there, and the final server records it as Return-Path. The From: header inside DATA is what people see, and it can differ, which is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
question: corp.example publishes p=reject. A message arrives with From: billing@corp.example, SPF pass for mailer.example (not aligned), and a DKIM signature from corp.example that fails because a gateway edited the body. What is the DMARC result?
options: Fail, because no passing mechanism is aligned
Pass, because SPF passed
Pass, because the DKIM domain aligns
None, because the signature was edited
explain: DMARC needs a pass that is also aligned. SPF passed but for an unaligned domain; DKIM is aligned but failed. Neither qualifies, so DMARC fails and p=reject applies. Edits in transit are a known source of legitimate DMARC failures.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and why passkeys resist it
question: A user on an AiTM phishing page enters their password and a correct six-digit TOTP code (time-based one-time password, the code an authenticator app shows). What does the attacker end up with?
options: Nothing, because the code expires in 30 seconds
Only the password, because MFA stops the login
The user's private key
A valid session cookie for the real site, obtained by relaying the code in time
explain: The proxy forwards the code immediately, while it is still valid. The real site completes the login and issues a session cookie, which the proxy keeps.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Alignment: which addresses a type is allowed to start at
question: On x86-64 Linux, which of these addresses is a legal start for a `double`?
options: 0x7ffc1018
0x7ffc1004
0x7ffc1012
0x7ffc100c
explain: A double has alignment 8, so the address must be a multiple of 8, meaning the low three bits are zero. 0x18 = 24 is a multiple of 8. 0x04 and 0x0c are only multiples of 4, and 0x12 = 18 is only even.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
question: You pass a Rust `struct Point { x: f32, y: f32, tag: u8 }` to a C function expecting `struct Point { float x; float y; uint8_t tag; }`. What must you add?
options: #[repr(C)]
Nothing, Rust always uses declaration order
#[repr(packed)]
#[repr(align(8))]
explain: Only #[repr(C)] guarantees the C algorithm: declaration order and C padding, giving the same 12 bytes. The default repr may reorder; packed would remove the tail padding C expects; align changes alignment but not order.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
question: Two models both miss every keypoint by 6 px on the same people. Model A's errors are on the face; model B's are on hips and knees. Which has higher OKS?
options: Model A, faces are small so errors matter less
They are equal, since distances are equal
Model B, because hips and knees have larger sigma so the same distance is penalized less
It depends only on the person's area
explain: With the same d and s, the similarity depends on kappa. Hip and knee sigmas (.107, .087) are three to four times the face sigmas (.025 to .035), so B keeps much higher similarities.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
question: Why does Lucene abandon the graph once it has visited more nodes than there are matching documents?
options: A flat scan costs one distance per match, a bound the walk has already exceeded, and it is exact
Lucene graphs cannot hold more nodes than the filter matches
Visiting too many nodes corrupts the HNSW index
The kNN filter is converted into a post_filter
explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching document. Once the walk has spent more distance computations than that, the graph is doing worse than a scan would, so Lucene switches to a plan with a known, bounded cost that is also exact.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall
question: A loop reads two cache lines sequentially, then jumps to a random place and reads two lines again, and so on. Why does the hardware prefetcher help very little here?
options: Prefetchers only work on writes
The prefetcher requires 64 consecutive lines before starting
Random jumps disable the cache
After the two misses that train it, the stream ends, so its predictions point at lines that will never be read
explain: Training takes about two misses, and by then this short run is over. The prefetcher's guesses past the end become wasted bandwidth, the same overshoot Intel's manual warns about for short arrays.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts
question: A systemd service runs `ExecStart=/home/dev/tools/agent` and its unit has no `User=` line. Developers can edit files in their home directories. What is the best fix?
options: Add `NoNewPrivileges=yes` to the unit
Make /home/dev/tools/agent mode 700
Move the binary to a root-owned directory and run the service as a dedicated unprivileged user
Restart the service less often
explain: Without User=, the service runs as root, so whoever controls the file controls root. Moving it to a root-owned path removes the write path, and running as its own user limits the damage even if something else goes wrong. NoNewPrivileges does not help when the process already is root.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 3: UAC bypass, vulnerable drivers, PrintNightmare
question: A user with a standard (non-admin) account runs a published UAC bypass. What happens?
options: They get SYSTEM
They get a high-integrity administrator token
Nothing useful: a standard user has no administrator token for the bypass to unlock
UAC is disabled for all users on the machine
explain: UAC bypasses skip the consent prompt between an administrator's filtered token and full token. A standard user has only one, unprivileged token. That is why standard accounts for daily work blunt this whole class.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Lateral movement channels and the logs each one leaves
question: On a file server you see 4624 type 3 from an admin account, then 7045 for a service called `XYZSVC` with an image path in `C:\Windows\`, then a process started by services.exe. What happened most likely?
options: Someone logged in at the console
A remote execution tool used SMB and a temporary service to run a command
A scheduled task ran
RDP session reconnected
explain: A network logon followed by a freshly installed service and a child of services.exe is the SMB-plus-service pattern (T1021.002 with T1569.002). Console logons are type 2, RDP is type 10, and scheduled tasks write their own events.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
question: You double the number of rollouts per step from 8 to 16 to 'make the labels more accurate', using hard estimation. Which error grows?
options: Correct steps labeled bad, because more rollouts mean more failures
Wrong steps labeled good, because more rollouts give a lucky recovery more chances to occur
Neither; HE labels converge to the truth as N grows
Both shrink equally
explain: HE marks a step good if any rollout succeeds. P(at least one recovery) = 1 - (1-r)^N rises with N, so wrong steps get marked good more often. Correct-step false negatives (1-q)^N fall. Math-Shepherd observed exactly this: larger N led to false positives.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
question: A thread in a 4-thread web server calls `chdir("/tmp")`, then another thread opens the relative path `log.txt`. Where does the file get opened?
options: In /tmp, because pthreads share CLONE_FS state such as the working directory
In the old working directory, because each thread keeps its own cwd
It depends on which CPU each thread runs on
The open fails because cwd changes are not allowed in multi-threaded programs
explain: pthread_create passes CLONE_FS, so the working directory is shared by all threads of the process. This is a real source of bugs: a library that calls chdir silently changes path resolution for every thread.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
question: Which workload benefits most from running more threads than cores?
options: Matrix multiplication that never blocks
A crawler where each request spends 95 percent of its time waiting on the network
A compression job reading from a RAM disk
A tight spin loop measuring time
explain: Threads that mostly wait free the core through voluntary switches, so extra threads overlap waiting with useful work. CPU-bound jobs gain nothing beyond the core count. (An event loop is the other way to get the same overlap with fewer threads.)

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Code size vs recall, and refinements: OPQ, fast scan, ScaNN
question: Your embeddings come from a model whose first 32 of 256 dimensions carry most of the variance. Plain PQ with M = 16 has poor recall. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase nprobe
Apply an OPQ rotation before PQ so variance is balanced across sub-spaces
Switch from ADC to SDC
Use k* = 16 instead of 256
explain: With the natural split, the first 2 sub-quantizers must represent most of the variance with 256 centroids each, while the rest waste bits. OPQ learns a rotation (for Gaussian data, Eigenvalue Allocation balances eigenvalue products) so each sub-space gets comparable energy. nprobe only matters for IVF list coverage.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
question: You run DSPy's BootstrapRS without passing a valset. It reports 0.92 on 50 training examples, and 0.81 on your test set. What most likely explains the gap?
options: The valset defaulted to the trainset, so demos were bootstrapped from and selected on the same examples
BootstrapRS always reports accuracy times 1.1
The test set must be mislabelled
Random search cannot overfit
explain: Per the DSPy docs the valset defaults to the trainset. The selected program contains demos drawn from those same examples and was chosen for scoring well on them, so its training score is optimistic. Pass a separate valset and keep a test set apart.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations
question: Why does the rotation part of the forward process use IGSO(3) instead of adding Gaussian noise to the nine entries of R?
options: IGSO(3) is faster to sample than a Gaussian
Because a Gaussian perturbation of the nine entries leaves a matrix that is not orthonormal, so it is not a rotation at all
Because rotations have nine degrees of freedom and Gaussians only model three
Because the loss must be invariant to global rotation
explain: SO(3) is a curved manifold embedded in 9-dimensional space. Adding independent Gaussian noise to the entries leaves the manifold: columns stop being orthonormal and the determinant stops being 1. IGSO(3) is the transition density of Brownian motion that stays on the manifold.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Lists, dictionaries and sets: counting what matters
question: You want to know whether an address appears in a list of 2 million known-bad addresses, checked once per log line. Which container should hold the bad addresses?
options: A list, because it keeps the order from the threat feed
A set, because membership checks do not slow down as it grows
A string with all addresses joined by commas
A list sorted alphabetically
explain: `x in some_list` compares against items one by one, so it gets slower as the list grows. A set (like dict keys) uses hashing to jump straight to the right slot. A joined string can also give false matches: `1.2.3.4` is inside `11.2.3.45`.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
question: Your detection searches web logs for a known-bad string and has never fired, but a colleague finds the string percent-encoded twice in last week's logs. What is the best fix?
options: Add the twice-encoded form as a second exact string
Decode each field repeatedly until it stops changing, then search the decoded text
Search only for the % character
Base64-encode the logs first
explain: Adding encoded variants one by one never ends: once, twice, mixed case hex, partial encoding. Normalizing the input to a fixed point and matching once covers all of them, with a round limit so hostile input cannot make you loop forever.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Testing your script so it does not fail silently
question: Why does test_enrich.py pass a FakeSession to lookup_hash instead of letting it call VirusTotal?
options: The real API does not support MD5
Tests should be fast, repeatable and offline: no quota, no key, and no failures caused by the network or by the service's data changing
pytest cannot import requests
Fakes make the code run in production too
explain: A test that depends on a live service fails for reasons unrelated to your code and spends real quota. Designing functions to receive their dependencies (here, the session) is what makes fakes possible.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
question: A shopping site has a 50 ms search budget, a stable catalog, and logs of queries paired with clicked products. Which expansion fits best?
options: query2doc with an LLM on every query
HyDE with Contriever
Pseudo-relevance feedback with 10 docs and 10 terms on every query
doc2query-style document expansion trained on the logged pairs
explain: Document expansion moves the model cost to indexing, so query latency stays close to plain BM25, and the click logs are exactly the (query, document) pairs it trains on. An LLM call per query alone exceeds 2 seconds in the query2doc measurements; PRF doubles the searches.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Decomposition: Self-Ask, least-to-most and sub-query evidence
question: Why can no single rewrite of the Orion question reliably retrieve d2 (Mira Patel earned a degree at Lakeside University)?
options: Because BM25 cannot handle long queries
Because d2 is too short
Because the words that identify d2, Mira Patel, are a bridge entity known only after the first hop
Because d2 has the same score as d4
explain: d2 is about Mira Patel, and the question never mentions Patel. Only after Q1 retrieves d1 does the name exist to put in a query. This is why multi-hop retrieval needs sequential decomposition, not a better single query.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Binary search plus rescoring: oversample, then re-rank
question: Why does binary quantization pair so naturally with rescoring, compared with int8 scalar quantization?
options: Binary distances are coarse with many ties, so a cheap wide first pass plus a precise second pass recovers most quality
Binary codes cannot be stored in RAM without rescoring
Rescoring is impossible with int8 vectors
Binary distances are biased upward, and rescoring subtracts the bias
explain: 1 bit per dimension loses a lot of ranking detail, so the first stage is best used as a filter. Rescoring works with int8 too (Hugging Face shows it), it just matters less there.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Extended RaBitQ, and binary quantization in real systems
question: An extended RaBitQ index stores 7-bit codes. Why does storing the most significant bits in a separate array speed up search?
options: The top bits form the 1-bit RaBitQ code, so a fast 1-bit estimate plus its bound can prune most candidates before the remaining 6 bits are read
It lets the index skip the random rotation
The most significant bits never change between queries
It halves the storage
explain: The top bit of each dimension equals the sign code. A cheap first pass on those bits, with the error bound, discards candidates that cannot qualify, and only survivors pay for the full-precision estimate.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
question: A voter's last log entry is (index 7, term 3). A candidate's last entry is (index 9, term 2). Does the voter grant its vote?
options: Yes, because the candidate's log is longer
No, because the voter's last term is higher
Yes, if the candidate's term number is higher than the voter's current term
Only if a majority already voted for the candidate
explain: Up to date is decided first by the last entry's term, and only by length when the terms are equal. Term 3 beats term 2, so the voter's log is more up to date and it refuses, however long the candidate's log is. A higher election term does not override this check.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
question: You raise k from 20 to 50 on a long-context model and recall@k rises from 80% to 90%, but end-to-end accuracy barely moves. Which explanation does Liu et al.'s case study support?
options: The retriever is broken, because recall should not rise with k
The reader saturates: it fails to use the extra, mostly mid-context documents, while cost and latency grow
Long-context models ignore everything after the first 20 documents by design
Accuracy can never exceed recall@20
explain: Liu et al. saw exactly this: reader accuracy saturated long before retriever recall did, with roughly 1% to 1.5% gain from 20 to 50 documents. More evidence in the window is not the same as evidence the model uses.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: The seven failure points and how to debug them
question: Asked "What are the key points in policies D1, D3 and D5?", the system summarizes D1 well and mentions D3 and D5 in one line each, although all three were in context. Which failure point fits, and what do Barnett et al. suggest?
options: FP 6 Incorrect Specificity; retrieve fewer chunks
FP 1 Missing Content; add documents
FP 3 Not in Context; raise the token budget
FP 7 Incomplete; ask such questions separately, one per document
explain: The information was in the context and available, yet the answer missed some of it: that is FP 7. The paper's own example is a question about documents A, B and C, and it suggests asking those separately.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
question: A z-scored feature has missing values filled with 0. What does the model effectively believe about those documents?
options: That they are the worst on this feature
That they are exactly average on this feature
That the feature is unknown
Nothing, zeros are ignored
explain: After z-scoring, 0 is the mean. Filling with 0 claims the document is average, which may be wildly optimistic (or pessimistic). Fill with a deliberate value and add an is-missing indicator if absence carries information.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
question: A run puts two grade 3 documents at ranks 1 and 2 (0 to 3 scale, g_max = 3). How much does the second one add to ERR?
options: 7/8 x 1/2 = 0.4375, the same as if rank 1 were junk
Nothing, ERR only counts the first relevant document
7 / log2(3) = 4.42, as in DCG
0.125 x 0.875 x 1/2 = 0.055, because most users already stopped at rank 1
explain: Only 1 - 7/8 = 0.125 of users reach rank 2, and of those 7/8 stop there, worth 1/2 each: 0.125 x 0.875 x 0.5 = 0.055. In DCG the duplicate would add a full 7 x 0.631. This diminishing return is the point of the cascade model.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
question: In an RDMA Reliable Connection, which component retransmits a lost packet?
options: The application, after a timeout
The kernel TCP stack on the sender
The sender's NIC hardware
The network switch
explain: The NIC implements the transport. For RC the hardware tracks packet sequence numbers and acknowledgements and retries on timeout; only when retries are exhausted does the application see an error completion. There is no TCP stack involved in InfiniBand or RoCE.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
question: A key-value store uses RDMA WRITE (no immediate) for requests into a server buffer. The server's CPU never notices new requests. Why?
options: WRITE requires an RNR retry first
A plain RDMA WRITE generates no completion or notification on the responder; the server must poll memory or the client must use WRITE with immediate
The rkey is wrong
WRITE only works on UD
explain: One-sided WRITE is invisible to the responder's CPU by design. Either poll a flag or length word in the buffer (FaRM style, relying on in-order placement) or use WRITE with immediate, which consumes a posted receive and produces a CQE.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
question: Why does the server compute Sec-WebSocket-Accept from the client's key instead of sending any fixed token?
options: To encrypt the rest of the session with the derived key
To choose the masking key for server frames
To prove the response came from a server that understood the WebSocket handshake, not a cache or plain HTTP server
To compress later frames
explain: The accept value is SHA-1 of key plus a fixed GUID, base64-encoded. Only a server that parsed the WebSocket request can produce it, so a stale cached response or an unaware server cannot accidentally complete the handshake. It is not used for encryption or masking.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: A UDP sender delta-encodes snapshot 110 against snapshot 100, but the client never received 100. What design prevents this?
options: Always delta against the immediately previous snapshot
Send each snapshot twice
Use larger packets
Delta only against the most recent snapshot the receiver has acked, falling back to a known initial state
explain: Fiedler's scheme: the receiver acks the latest snapshot it has, and the sender encodes against the newest acked baseline. Before any ack, it encodes against the initial state both sides know.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
question: Why does YouTube's ranker weight clicked impressions by watch time instead of predicting click probability?
options: Watch time is easier to log than clicks
Logistic regression cannot learn click probabilities
Click probability rewards deceptive videos that users do not finish; weighting by watch time makes the learned odds approximate expected watch time
Weighting makes the model train faster
explain: Covington et al. say ranking by click-through rate promotes deceptive videos users do not complete (clickbait), while watch time better captures engagement. The weighting makes the odds approximately E[T](1 + P).

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: ArUco markers, camera calibration and solvePnP
question: You only need to measure flat objects lying next to a marker, and your lens has negligible distortion near the image center. What is the minimum you need?
options: A full calibration with 10 or more chessboard views, then solvePnP
The marker's 4 detected corners and its physical side length, then a homography to mm
The camera's focal length from the phone's EXIF data (the camera metadata saved inside the photo file), then similar triangles
Two photos from different positions for stereo depth
explain: For points on the marker's plane, the plane-to-image map is a homography and the 4 corners plus the known side length determine it. Intrinsics enter only when you need 3D pose or must remove lens distortion. A focal length alone does not give Z.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
question: A query has `GROUP BY model ORDER BY model` and there is a B-tree index on model. Which plan shape avoids both a hash table and an explicit Sort?
options: Seq Scan, then HashAggregate, then Sort
Seq Scan, then Sort, then HashAggregate
Bitmap Heap Scan, then HashAggregate
Index Scan in model order, then GroupAggregate
